events.text: Straw, and dark, and a roar that never stops. The straw is still warm in a great hollow beside you, the shape of something far bigger than you that lay here until tonight and is not here now. Up through the rock comes the sound of a bell. Down through the cave mouth comes the sound of water breaking white on stones. You have four legs. None of them has agreed to anything yet.
events.arc: The Cave Under the Nine-Step Palace

choices.text: Stand up

effects.log: Front legs, then back legs, then front legs again, because the back ones were not listening. You stand in the straw, swaying. Nobody sees it. It counts anyway.

choices.text: Put your nose in the warm hollow

effects.log: It smells of cloud, and old hay, and something like the air before snow. It is the smell of the one who should be here. You lie down in the hollow. It is much too big. You fit in the middle of it like a chestnut in a bowl.

choices.text: Listen to the water below

effects.log: It never stops talking. It says the same thing over and over in a white voice, and you will spend a long time learning that what it says is: go round, go round, go round.

events.text: Every night the hollow in the straw is a little colder and smells a little less of the one who lay in it. The great prints at the cave mouth, pressed in the dust, have begun to blur where the wind comes in. Nobody comes back. You are beginning to understand that nobody was ever going to.
events.arc: The Cave Under the Nine-Step Palace

choices.text: Drag the straw into a heap to keep the smell in

effects.log: You push it together with your nose all night. In the morning the heap smells of you. You stand looking at it for a long time. Then you lie down in it, because it is warm, and that is what a heap of straw is for.

choices.text: Lie on the prints in the dust so the wind cannot take them

effects.log: You lie across them for three nights. The wind goes round you. On the fourth night you get up to drink and the wind has them in an hour. Some things you cannot keep by lying on them. (-2 health)

choices.text: Let it go: the wind is doing what wind does

effects.log: The smell goes. The prints go. The straw is only straw. You find you can breathe more easily in a cave that is only a cave.

events.text: At night the rapids under the cliff go white, and when the moon is on them, silver: a long rope of moving light going round black stones. The monks of the temple above call it the White Silver Rapids. You do not know the name. You only know you cannot stop looking at it.
events.arc: The Cave Under the Nine-Step Palace

choices.text: Watch where the water goes round the stones

effects.log: It never breaks a stone. It goes round them, over them, past them, for ten thousand years, and the stones are round because of it. You watch until the moon goes down, learning something you cannot say yet.

choices.text: Go down the slope to the edge and touch it with one hoof

ok.log: Cold enough to make your whole body jump. The water closes round your soft hoof and lets it go again, and leaves it clean. You go back up very proud of yourself.

fail.log: The slope is wet moss and you are new. You slide the last few feet and sit down in the shallows with a splash, and the cold takes your breath. You climb out shaking and climb back up shaking. (-5 health)

choices.text: Sleep with your head toward the sound

effects.log: From then on you always sleep that way. Wherever you lie down, all your life, some part of you turns toward running water.

events.text: The path down from the cave mouth is a goat track between ferns, and after the night rain it is covered in snails. Dozens of them, out on the wet stones with their horns up, going nowhere slowly. Below is the meadow and the dew and breakfast. Between you and breakfast, the snails.
events.arc: The Cave Under the Nine-Step Palace

choices.text: Pick a way down between them, hoof by hoof

effects.log: It takes the whole morning. You look before every step, and twice you have to stand on three legs for a long time while a snail decides. You reach the meadow when the dew is gone. You are hungry and you have not broken a single shell. (-2 health)

choices.text: Go down the quick way over the moss (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Crack. A small sound under your back hoof, smaller than a twig. You do not stop. You eat in the meadow, and the dew is sweet, and the crack goes on in your ears all day, louder than the rapids. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Wait in the cave mouth until the sun sends them in

effects.log: By noon the stones are dry and every snail is back under the ferns. You walk down a clean path and eat late. The snails, for their part, never knew you were waiting.

events.text: You are too big for the cave now. You knock your head on the low place every morning, and the straw does not cover your back. The forest below the cliff is full of the smell of roe deer, and the temple bell, and the river. This morning you stand in the cave mouth and do not go back in.
events.arc: The Cave Under the Nine-Step Palace

choices.text: Go down into the forest and do not look back

effects.log: Down the goat track, across the meadow, into the oaks. The cave stays in the cliff behind you, a dark mouth over white water, and you do not turn round. You know where it is. You will always know where it is.

choices.text: Look back once from the meadow

effects.log: A dark mouth in the cliff, under the temple roof, over the rapids. The place you were left. You will come back to it, more than once. The last time, you will not be coming back to sleep.

choices.text: Leave a heap of fresh straw in the hollow, in case

effects.log: You carry windblown straw up from the meadow all morning and heap it in the old hollow. In case. You do not finish the thought.

events.text: In the straw where the old one lay, tangled round a stalk, there is a ribbon. Faded silk, embroidered once with flowers that are now only threads. It is not new. It is not from tonight. Something tells you, the way the river tells you which way is down, that it was tied to a horn by a human hand at a gate somewhere, long ago, and that it was tied for you.

choices.text: Lift it out of the straw with your teeth

effects.log: It is light as a breath. You do not know what to do with it, so you lay it on the stone at the back of the cave where the drips cannot reach it, and you look at it every night. One day there will be a horn to tie it to. Not yet.

choices.text: Lie down with your nose on it

effects.log: It smells of nothing now. Of a hand, maybe. Of a birth in a house at dusk, and an old woman saying you must. You sleep with your nose on it and dream of a gate.

events.text: The monks above the cave are talking about a lord's hunt, the way old men talk about weather. Long ago, they say, a lord took a strange beast in the west with a broken foreleg, and someone in his train set its leg and took it out of his hands. The lord was furious. The beast went free. "Since then," says the oldest monk, "they say the age has been a little kinder." You do not know why it makes your foreleg ache.

choices.text: Stretch the foreleg, slowly

effects.log: It is whole. Someone, somewhere, set a leg like it once and carried a beast out of a courtyard full of men who did not know what it was. The age you are born into is a little kinder for it. (The Times: a quieter age)

choices.text: Listen to the rest of the story

effects.log: The lord made an enemy that day, and kept it all his life. The one who set the leg never cared. The monks argue about whether the beast was real. You lie in the straw under them, and do not argue. (The Times: a quieter age)

events.text: The monks above the cave are talking about a lord's hunt. Long ago, they say, a lord took a strange beast in the west with a broken foreleg, and a famous guest told him it was an omen of his glory, and he kept it, and it died in his courtyard, and an old scholar in the crowd wept into his sleeve and never forgave anyone. "Since then," says the oldest monk, "lords have hunted every strange thing they see."

choices.text: Press yourself into the back of the cave

effects.log: You do not know why your heart is going like a rabbit. Somewhere in a life that was not yours, someone told a lord what he wanted to hear. The age you are born into remembers it. (The Times: a harder age)

choices.text: Listen to the old scholar part again

effects.log: The scholar wept into his sleeve, the monk says, and said his way was at an end. You lie very still in the straw. Something in you knows the sleeve. (The Times: a harder age)

events.text: The monks above the cave are talking about a war that ended in a day. Long ago, they say, a lord's war in the west stopped between one dawn and the next, because someone who could stop it did, so that a hurt beast in the lord's courtyard could be let go into a peace, "because it cannot live anywhere else". The oldest monk laughs. "A war ended for an animal. Nobody believes it. And yet the roads have been safe since."

choices.text: Believe it

effects.log: You believe it with your whole small body. Somebody once ended a war so that something like you could walk out of a courtyard into a quiet country. You are born into what is left of that quiet. (The Times: an age of peace)

choices.text: Go to the cave mouth and look at the safe roads

effects.log: Far below, a carter on the river road, alone, singing, with no guard and no sword. The monk is right. Nobody believes it. The roads do. (The Times: an age of peace)

events.text: The oldest monk above the cave tells the novices a story at dawn, after the bell. Long ago, he says, the Jade court in heaven argued whether the benevolent beast should come down to the world at all, in an age like this one. One immortal stood up and said: it should, because if it only comes when the age is good, it only comes when nobody needs it. "And so," says the monk, "it came." The novices laugh. In the straw below them, you do not.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to the end

effects.log: Somebody in heaven spoke for you before you were born. The age you are born into is a little kinder for the coming. (The Times: a quieter age)

choices.text: Answer the bell, once, softly

effects.log: The novices stop laughing. The old monk smiles at the floor. "You see," he says. (The Times: a quieter age)

events.text: The oldest monk above the cave tells the novices a story at dawn. Long ago, he says, the Jade court argued whether the benevolent beast should come down to the world, and an immortal who had seen what the world does with such things said: it must wait above. "So it waited," says the monk, "and the world went on without it, and got worse. When it came at last, it came late, into a hard age."

choices.text: Press yourself into the back of the cave

effects.log: Someone in heaven was afraid for you, and was right to be, and the waiting cost the world. You are born into what the waiting left. (The Times: a harder age)

choices.text: Listen for what came after

effects.log: "After?" says the monk to a novice. "Hunters, mostly." You lie very still in the straw. (The Times: a harder age)

events.text: The oldest monk above the cave tells the novices a story at dawn. Long ago, he says, an immortal stood up in the Jade court and said: give me a hundred years, and I will make the world fit for the benevolent beast before it comes down. "And it was done," says the monk. "Without a killing. They say that is why the roads are safe."

choices.text: Believe it

effects.log: Somebody spent a hundred years making a world for you to be born into. You are born into it. (The Times: an age of peace)

choices.text: Go to the cave mouth and look at the quiet valley

effects.log: Smoke from cooking fires, a carter singing on the river road, nobody armed. A hundred years of someone else's work, lying in the morning sun. (The Times: an age of peace)

events.text: Before the cave mouth, at the top of the slope above the rapids, there is a flat stone, and in the stone there are hoofprints. Not pressed in mud: pressed in rock, deep as a bowl, as if the rock had been soft for one night. They go to the edge of the stone and stop. There are no prints after them. There is only the sky.

choices.text: Put your hoof in one

effects.log: Your hoof sits in the bottom of it like a pebble in a well. It is far, far too big. You stand there with one leg in the print and three on the stone, and something in your chest goes very quiet and very large.

choices.text: Follow them to the edge and look up

effects.log: They stop at the edge. You stop at the edge. You look up for a long time, at the place where the next print would be if there were anything to print on. A cloud goes by. That is all.

choices.text: Drink the rainwater pooled in the last print

effects.log: It has the taste of stone and of something else, faint, like cold air high up. You drink every drop and then feel you should not have, and then feel that you were meant to.

events.text: {npc}, the monk with the dew bowl, finds you standing in the great print on the stone at dawn. {He} sets the bowl down and sits on the edge of the stone with {his} old knees cracking. "The first king of this country kept a horse in that cave," {he} says, to nobody. "A horse that was not a horse. At the end the king rode it up from this stone to heaven, and it never came back. Neither did the king. The temple calls it the Morning-Heaven Stone."

choices.text: Stay in the print while {he} talks

effects.log: {npc} tells it all: the king, the cave, the stone, the morning. {He} does not look at you once. When {he} is finished {he} picks up the empty bowl and says, "Some say it left a foal." Then {he} goes back up the steps.

choices.text: Step out of the print, as if caught

effects.log: You step out quickly. {npc} laughs, a short dry laugh like a broom on stone. "Go on," {he} says. "It is your stone more than mine." {He} tells you the story anyway, while you stand beside the print pretending not to listen.

choices.text: Drink the dew first: stories keep

effects.log: You drink. {npc} waits. Then {he} tells it, the first king and the strange horse and the morning it went up and did not come back, and you hear every word with dew on your chin.

events.text: Full moon. You come up from the forest to the Morning-Heaven Stone, as you do on full-moon nights now, and lie down with your chin in the largest of the old prints. Your forehead itches where a horn will be one day. The rapids below are silver. You think, the way you think nothing else, about going up.

choices.text: Promise the stone you will come back here when you are ready

effects.log: You do not know ready for what. You promise anyway, under the moon, with your chin in the print. Many years from now, on this stone, you will swear something much larger. It begins tonight, as a promise to a rock.

choices.text: Try to leave a print of your own

ok.log: You stamp until your soft hooves ache, and in the morning there is, if you look hard, a scratch on the stone beside the great prints. It may be yours. It may have been there before. You decide it is yours.

fail.log: Rock is rock. You stamp until your hooves are sore and the stone does not notice. Whatever made those prints was something you are not yet. (-4 health)

choices.text: Sleep there until the dew

effects.log: You sleep on the stone with the moon on you and wake wet with dew and very cold, with the bell ringing above. You feel as if someone stood over you in the night. Nobody did. Probably.

events.text: A beetle on its back on the cave floor, legs going in the air like someone rowing a boat with no water under it. It is black and shiny and very busy and getting nowhere. You put your nose down close. It smells of earth and panic.

choices.text: Turn it over with your nose, gently

effects.log: It takes four tries. Your nose is too big and too soft and the beetle keeps grabbing it. On the fourth it rolls over, rights itself, and walks off without a word, as if it had been on its back on purpose.

choices.text: Paw at it to see what it does (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: It does what anything does under a hoof: it breaks. One leg comes away. It rights itself in the struggle and limps off on five. You stand looking at the leg on the stone for a long time. Nobody told you. You know anyway. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Watch it until it rights itself

effects.log: It takes most of the afternoon. It catches a straw at last and pulls itself over, and goes, and you are absurdly proud of it, as if you had done it.

events.text: An ant road across the cave mouth: a line of them, both ways, from a crack in the stone to the ferns outside, carrying crumbs and eggs and each other. It is exactly where you need to put your feet to go out. They were here first. They have been here, from the look of the path worn in the stone, for a thousand years.

choices.text: Step over, very high

ok.log: One leg, very high, very slowly. Then the next. You stand on the far side, trembling, and the ant road has not even noticed you. That is exactly what you wanted.

fail.log: Your back hoof is not as clever as your front one. It comes down a hair short. You do not look. You know. The road closes over the gap in a breath, as if nothing happened, and that is somehow worse. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Wait until they are gone (this may take some time)

effects.log: They are not gone at noon. They are not gone at dusk. They are a road, not a crowd. You sleep in the cave mouth with your nose a hand from them and go out at dawn, when the cold has sent them in. (-3 health)

choices.text: Find another way out, over the back rocks

effects.log: There is a crack at the back of the cave that comes out above the ferns, if you are small and do not mind skin off your knees. You are small. You mind. You go anyway. (-3 health)

events.text: You cross the meadow below the cliff at dawn and look back, as you have started doing. Your tracks show dark in the dew. And there, in the middle of them, one blade of grass lies folded over, flat, the way it has never lain before. You did that. It was not on purpose. It does not seem to matter to the blade.

choices.text: Go back and try to lift it with your lips

ok.log: You take the tip in your lips as softly as you have ever done anything and lift. It comes up. It stands. It is a little crooked for the rest of the summer, and you visit it every morning, and it lives.

fail.log: It snaps at the fold, a sound so small only you could hear it. You stand over the two halves of it until the dew is gone. It was one blade in a meadow of ten thousand. It was the one you broke. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Stand beside it and wait for it to rise by itself

effects.log: It takes until noon. Slowly, the way an old man gets up from a mat, it comes back up, bent at the middle, standing. It was only bent, not broken. You learn the difference that morning and never forget it.

choices.text: Walk on, and watch your feet from now on

effects.log: You do not go back. You go forward more slowly, looking down. By the end of the meadow your tracks in the dew show nothing folded at all. It is not the same as mending it. It is what you can do.

events.text: Rain all night, and in the morning the whole path to the chestnut trees is alive: snails, worms, a frog the size of your hoof, and a toad the size of two. You are very hungry. The chestnuts that fell in the night are lying under the trees, and the squirrels are already among them.

choices.text: Walk it anyway, fast (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You get the chestnuts before the squirrels. You do not look at the path on the way back. You do not need to: you heard it. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Carry them off the path one by one in your lips

effects.log: The toad objects. The frog objects. The worms do not have opinions. By the time the path is clear the squirrels have had the chestnuts. You eat dew off the leaves instead, and feel strangely rich. (-3 health)

choices.text: Go hungry until the path dries

effects.log: By afternoon the path is dry and empty and so is the ground under the chestnut trees. You lick the dew off the leaves. It is not breakfast. It is not nothing. (-4 health)

events.text: Spring, and the meadow is new, every blade standing. You stand at the edge of it at dawn and decide something. This year, from this morning to the next first frost, nothing under your feet. Not a beetle, not a snail, not a blade. One whole year. The monks would call it a vow. You do not have the word. You have only the feet.

choices.text: Walk only on stones and roots this year

effects.log: Stone to root to stone. You learn every flat rock on the ridge and every root of the old chestnuts. It is slow, and your legs ache in new places. (If nothing is harmed by the first frost, the Feet are yours.)

choices.text: Walk only at dawn, when you can see everything

effects.log: In the grey light before sunrise the ground shows you everything: the snail, the shoot, the nest in the grass. You walk then, and lie still the rest of the day. (If nothing is harmed by the first frost, the Feet are yours.)

choices.text: Lie still in the cave all year: nothing can be crushed by a foal lying down

effects.log: Nothing is crushed. Nothing is learned either. The Feet are not a thing you can get by lying in the straw. Next year, you think. Next year you will walk.

events.text: You walk through the oak wood at dusk and a roe doe twenty paces off does not lift her head. A hare under a fern does not move. You are behind a woodcutter on the path for a whole li before he sneezes, turns, and sits down hard on the ground. Your feet have learned something your head has not caught up with.

choices.text: Walk up to the woodcutter, slowly

effects.log: He sits in the path with his axe across his knees and his mouth open while a grey-gold thing with soft hooves walks round him, not touching a leaf, and goes on. He tells his wife he saw a deer made of mist. She tells him to stop eating mushrooms off the old pine.

choices.text: Go back the way you came, unseen

effects.log: He never sees you. He goes home and says the wood was strange today, as if something was walking just behind him and the leaves were holding their breath. He is right.

events.text: At dawn, after the bell, a monk comes down the steps from the temple with a wooden bowl held in both hands. {npc} is grey-robed and bony and walks the way people walk carrying something full. {He} sets the bowl on the stone at the cave mouth, does not look into the cave, and goes back up. The bowl is full of dew, gathered drop by drop off lotus leaves.
events.arc: The Monk With the Dew Bowl

choices.text: Drink it when {he} has gone

effects.log: It tastes of lotus and of the morning. Tomorrow the bowl is there again. And the next day. {npc} never once looks into the cave. You understand, later, that not looking was the gift too.

choices.text: Come out and drink while {he} is still there

effects.log: {npc} stops on the third step and does not turn round. You drink. The old shoulders shake a little: laughing, or the other thing. "Good," {he} says to the steps. "Good." The bowl is there every dawn after that.

choices.text: Follow {him} up the steps to see where it comes from

ok.log: A lotus pond in a temple court, and {npc} with a ladle, tipping each broad leaf so its one drop of dew rolls into the bowl. A hundred leaves for one bowl. You go back down the steps before {he} sees you, and from then on you drink very slowly.

fail.log: You get four steps up and your soft hooves slip on the moss and you come down the four steps faster than you went up. {npc} does not turn round. "Not yet," {he} says to the steps. You drink the dew, bruised. (-3 health)

events.text: {npc} has started sitting on the bottom step after setting down the bowl, with {his} back to the cave, and reciting. Always the same old verse, three short parts, about the feet of something, and its forehead, and its horn. "The feet of the lin," {he} says to the rapids. "The forehead of the lin. The horn of the lin." Then {he} explains it, as if the rapids had asked.
events.arc: The Monk With the Dew Bowl

choices.text: Listen to the part about the feet

effects.log: "Its feet do not tread on a living thing," {npc} tells the rapids. "Not an insect. Not a blade of grass." You look down at your own feet. They look back, soft and grey-gold and full of opinions about beetles.

choices.text: Listen to the part about the forehead

effects.log: "Its forehead is never thrust forward in wrath," says {npc}. "It is struck, and it does not butt." You rub your forehead on the cave wall where it itches. You do not know yet that this is the hard one.

choices.text: Listen to the part about the horn

effects.log: "Its horn ends in flesh," says {npc}. "It has the power to wound, and it does not use it." Then, quietly, to {him}self: "The old books argue whether it is a qi or a lin. I think the books can argue." {He} picks up the bowl and goes.

events.text: Behind the temple, {npc} sweeps the stone steps every morning with a broom of bush clover. You watch from the ferns. {He} sweeps round the ant roads. {He} lifts a caterpillar off a step on the end of a leaf and sets it in the moss. Then one morning, without turning, {he} says: "You can come out. I know what you are. I only do not know what you are for."
events.arc: The Monk With the Dew Bowl

choices.text: Come out and stand on the step below {him}

mem.note: came out and stood by me

effects.log: {npc} sweeps round you as round an ant road, and goes on talking. "Nor do I," {he} says, "know what I am for. Fifty years of sweeping. Perhaps it was for this morning." You stand still and let {him} sweep round you. It is the first human you have stood next to.

choices.text: Stay in the ferns: you do not know what you are for either

effects.log: {npc} nods to the ferns. "Good answer," {he} says, which is a strange thing to say to silence. You think about it all day. You are a thing that does not know what it is for. It feels, oddly, like a place to start.

choices.text: Pick up a fallen leaf and lay it on the step for {him} to sweep

mem.note: gave me a leaf to sweep

effects.log: {npc} looks at the leaf for a long time, then sweeps it off the step with great ceremony. "Thank you," {he} says. "I was running out." From then on there is a leaf on the bottom step every morning.

events.text: The dew bowl comes later every morning. {npc}'s knees have gone; {he} takes the steps one at a time, sideways, with a hand on the rock. This morning the bowl does not come at all. At noon you find {him} sitting halfway down the steps with the bowl in {his} lap, spilled, looking at the rapids, quite calm, unable to get up.
events.arc: The Monk With the Dew Bowl

choices.text: Lie down on the step below, so {he} can lean on you

mem.note: let me lean on you on the steps

effects.log: It takes the whole afternoon to go up thirty steps: {npc} leaning on your back, you moving one step, waiting, the next. At the top {he} pats your neck once. "Well," {he} says. "Now we each know what the other is for." (-4 health)

choices.text: Go up and bring the other monks

ok.log: You stand in the temple court among the lotus jars until a young monk sees you and drops a broom. Then another. You turn and go to the steps and look back, twice, until they understand and follow. They carry {npc} up. Nobody in that temple ever forgets the morning the strange deer came for help.

fail.log: The young monks see you in the court and shout and run, and by the time you have led anyone anywhere {npc} has got {him}self up the steps alone, very slowly, laughing at all of you. (-3 health)

choices.text: Fetch dew yourself, from the lotus leaves, and bring it to {him}

effects.log: You tip each lotus leaf with your nose the way you saw {him} do it, and carry the bowl down in your teeth. Half of it spills. {npc} drinks what is left, and cries a little, and says it is the dew.

events.text: The bell does not ring at dawn. The temple is quiet, and then, from the cell at the end of the court, there is the sound of a wooden clapper, slow, and young voices chanting. You know before you go up. {npc} is lying on a thin mat by the open door, very small, and {his} eyes find you in the courtyard at once.
events.arc: The Monk With the Dew Bowl

choices.text: Go to the door and put your head in

mem.note: came to my door at the end

effects.log: The young monks pull back against the walls. {npc} lifts one hand and puts it on your forehead, where the horn will be. "The feet, the forehead, the horn," {he} says. "You have the first. Get the others." Then {he} is gone, and the clapper stops. You stay in the door until the sun is high.

choices.text: Stand in the court where {he} can see you, and do not come closer

effects.log: {npc} watches you through the door until {his} eyes close. You do not go in. You do not need to. Afterwards you understand that you have been to a deathbed, and that it is a thing you will do again, many times, for people you have not met yet.

choices.text: Ring the bell for {him}, since nobody has

ok.log: You put your shoulder to the log beam and swing it, and the bell speaks over the whole valley, late, once. In the cell {npc} smiles at the sound and goes with it. The young monks write in the temple record that the bell rang itself.

fail.log: The beam is too heavy and only knocks the bell, a dull small sound. It is enough. {npc} hears it and smiles and goes. You have a bruise on your shoulder the shape of a bell beam for a month. (-5 health)

events.text: In the middle of the night someone is sweeping the cave. A broom, slow, swish and swish, across the straw. You lift your head. There is a man by the back wall in a plain hemp jacket, old, bent, with a broom of twigs. You can see the rock through him. He sweeps the old hollow in the straw very carefully, the way you would tidy a bed someone has just got up from.

choices.text: Lie very still and watch

effects.log: He sweeps until the moon leaves the cave mouth. Then he leans the broom on nothing, and there is no broom, and no man. The straw in the hollow is a little straighter than it was.

choices.text: Get up and go to him

effects.log: He stops sweeping. He looks at you a long time. "Small," he says, in a voice like dry straw. "You are very small. He was the height of a gate." He goes back to sweeping, but he sweeps round you now, as you would round a sleeping foal.

choices.text: Hide under the straw

effects.log: He sweeps right up to the edge of your heap and stops, and you hear him chuckle. "I know," he says. "I know. I hid from him too, the first night." Then the sweeping goes away down the cave and is gone.

events.text: The ghost with the broom comes most nights now, and talks while he sweeps. He was the groom, he says, of the horse that was not a horse, the one that lived in this cave, for the first king of this country. Thirty years he carried its straw and combed its mane. "And then one morning the king said, saddle it, and I did, and he rode it out on the stone and up. Up," says the groom. "It never came back. Neither did he."

choices.text: Ask what it was like

effects.log: "Like you," says the groom, "but finished. Scales of every colour. A horn with a soft end. It never once kicked me, and I gave it reason." He sweeps a while. "It used to stop for ants," he says. "The king hated waiting."

choices.text: Ask why he is still here

effects.log: "Somebody has to sweep," says the groom. "In case." He does not say in case of what. You do not ask. You both know.

choices.text: Ask if it will come back

effects.log: The groom stops sweeping. "I thought so," he says. "For a long time. Then you came. A horse does not leave a foal in a cave if it is coming back." He goes on sweeping, much more slowly.

events.text: The groom is fainter every year. Tonight you can hardly see the broom, only hear it. "I am tired," he says. "Thirty years alive and I do not know how many dead, sweeping for a horse that went up. Will you do something for me? If you ever go up, the way it went, and you see it: tell it the straw is still swept."

choices.text: Promise

effects.log: "Good," says the groom, and sweeps the hollow one last time, and puts the broom against the wall, and this time the broom stays: an old twig broom, real, leaning on the rock. He is not there. You will carry the message a very long way.

choices.text: Tell him he can stop now: you will keep the straw

effects.log: He looks at you, small as you are, and laughs, and the laugh goes out like a lamp. The broom falls over in the straw. In the morning the hollow is untidy for the first time in a thousand years. You tidy it. Badly.

choices.text: Ask him to stay a little longer

effects.log: "A little," he says. He stays the winter. In the spring he is only a sound of sweeping some nights, and then not even that, and there is a twig broom against the wall that was not there before. You do not know when you promised. You did.

events.text: Wolves. Three of them, grey, from the pines on Peony Peak, coming down the slope toward the stream where you are drinking, low and not hurrying, because they can see you are alone and small and have soft feet. You have no horn. You have never had to run from anything this size. Behind you are the rapids.

choices.text: Run for the rapids

ok.log: Into the white water, onto a stone, onto the next, and the current takes the place where you were. The wolves stop at the edge. They pace. They do not like the noise. You stand on a black stone in the middle of the roaring, shaking, safe.

fail.log: Teeth close on your hind leg on the bank and let go as you hit the water. You go under, and up, and onto a stone. The wolves pace on the bank. You stand bleeding into the white water until they give up at dark. (-12 health)

choices.text: Stand perfectly still

effects.log: They circle. They sniff. The biggest one puts its nose to yours, and you do not move, and something in the way you stand puzzles it: you are not prey, quite, and not anything else it knows. It snaps once at your flank and leads them off. (-8 health)

choices.text: Kick out at the lead wolf (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your soft hoof catches its muzzle and something in it gives. It yelps and backs off, and the others with it. You are alive. On the stone where it stood there is blood that is not yours. You look at it longer than you looked at the wolves. (Bent +3; -6 health)

events.text: You go back to the rapids every day after that and learn them: which black stones hold, which roll, which are only foam pretending. The wolves come to the bank sometimes and watch you. You stand in the middle of the white water where they cannot follow and look back at them. Nobody fights. Nobody eats anybody. It is a kind of conversation.

choices.text: Learn every stone in the rapids

effects.log: By autumn you can cross from bank to bank in the dark without wetting your knees. The water still roars. You hear, now, the stones under it: go here, not here, here. The rapids were always a road. Nobody else was light enough to use it.

choices.text: Lie down on the big stone and let the wolves watch

effects.log: You lie down in the middle of the rapids with spray on your back. The wolves lie down on the bank. You stay like that until dusk, two kinds of patience across the white water, and then they go home and so do you.

events.text: Spring melt. The rapids are high and brown and very loud. On the bank the wolves are howling, all of them, the she-wolf with one eye running up and down at the edge, because a cub has gone in. It is in the white water by the big stone, going round and round in the backwash, its head going under and coming up smaller each time.

choices.text: Go out on the stones and push it to the bank

ok.log: Stone, stone, the big stone, and you get your head under the cub and shove. It goes up the bank in a wet heap at the one-eyed wolf's feet. She looks at you over it, her whole body shaking. Then she picks it up by the neck and goes.

fail.log: The current takes your legs on the big stone and you go in with the cub. You come up with it against your chest and the two of you hit the bank together, half drowned. The one-eyed wolf takes it out of the water. She does not bite you. (-12 health)

choices.text: Stay on the bank: they are the wolves who hunted you

effects.log: The cub goes under and does not come up. The one-eyed wolf stands at the edge all night. It was not your doing. You did not do anything. You lie awake a long time trying to make those two sentences mean the same thing.

choices.text: Stand in the backwash so the water piles against you and sends the cub out

effects.log: You plant yourself in the white water and it breaks on you instead of turning, and the cub spins out of the eddy into the shallows. You stand there in the cold until the she-wolf has it. Your legs do not stop shaking until night. (-8 health)

events.text: A hard winter. You meet the pack on the ridge path above the rapids, in deep snow, and there is no stone and no water, only you and seven hungry wolves. One of them is young and very large. The old she-wolf with one eye walks out of the pack and stands between it and you, and does not look at either of you.

choices.text: Walk past, slowly

effects.log: You walk past the whole pack in the snow. Not one moves. The big young one, the cub from the rapids, looks after you with something in its yellow eyes that is not hunger. It does not know what it is either.

choices.text: Bow your head to the one-eyed wolf

effects.log: She looks at you then, once, with her one eye, and turns away. A debt, paid in the only coin wolves have: not eating you. The forest is a place of very strict accounts.

events.text: Boys on the wall above the temple lane. Four of them, with pockets full of stones, and the strange grey deer that comes down to the spring is the best target that has ever walked into their lane. The first stone hits your flank. The second hits your forehead, right where it itches.

choices.text: Stand there and let them

effects.log: Five stones, six. You do not move. The smallest boy stops first, with a stone in his fist, looking at you. Then the next. The biggest throws two more, alone, and then he stops too, because it is not fun to throw at something that only looks at you. (-6 health)

choices.text: Run back up the lane

effects.log: Stones bounce off the walls behind you. The boys cheer. You drink at the spring that night instead, in the dark, when nobody is on the wall. Running is not harm. It is also not anything else.

choices.text: Butt the nearest boy off the wall (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You go up the bank and your forehead catches him in the shins and he goes over backwards into the vegetable patch. He breaks his arm. The other three run screaming that the deer is a demon. Nobody throws stones in that lane again. (Bent +3)

events.text: There is a billy goat on the path to the spring. Big, shaggy, yellow-eyed, with horns curled like a scholar's ear-trumpet, and it belongs to nobody, and it has decided that the path to the spring is its path. The first morning, it lowers its head and runs at you and hits you square on the forehead.

choices.text: Stand and take it, and come back tomorrow

effects.log: It hits you, backs off, hits you again. You stand. It stops, puzzled, and goes off to eat a fence. Tomorrow you come back. So does it. This will go on, you can tell, for some time. (-10 health)

choices.text: Butt it back, once (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You lower your head and meet it. Its skull rings. It staggers off with blood on its forehead and does not come back to the path. You drink at the spring. The water tastes of nothing at all. (Bent +3)

choices.text: Take the long way round to the spring

effects.log: There is a long way round, over a ridge, through brambles. It takes all morning. The goat watches you go with satisfaction. You both know who won. You are not sure it matters.

events.text: A soldier on the road below the temple, reeling from the tavern at the ford with a bamboo staff, and you are standing in his road because an ant road crosses it and you are waiting. He does not see ants. He sees a deer that will not move. He starts to beat you with the staff.

choices.text: Do not move, and do not answer

effects.log: The staff comes down on your back, your neck, your forehead. You stand over the ant road and take it. At last he stops, out of breath, and looks at what he has been hitting, and at the ants, and sits down in the road. In the morning he cannot look at you. The Forehead: the second verse is yours. (-12 health)

choices.text: Step off the road and let the ants take their chances

effects.log: You step aside. He stumbles past cursing and his boots go through the ant road like a cart through a village. You stand on the verge and watch the ants put it back together. You did not do it. You let it be done.

choices.text: Knock him into the ditch with your shoulder (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: He goes into the ditch and stays there, groaning, with a cut head. The ants go on. You go on. In the morning he tells the village a demon deer attacked him on the road, and for once it is true. (Bent +3)

events.text: The thirty-first morning. The billy goat is on the path, as it has been every morning for a month. Your forehead has a sore place on it that never quite heals. The goat lowers its head. And then it does not run. It stands and looks at you, for a long time, with its yellow eyes.

choices.text: Stand and wait

effects.log: It looks. You wait. At last it snorts, turns round, and walks off down the hill to eat somebody's washing, and it never stands on that path again. You did not win. It gave up. The Forehead: the second verse is yours.

choices.text: Lower your head, the way it does, but do not run

effects.log: Two heads lowered, a pace apart, in the morning. Nobody moves. Then the goat sighs through its nose like an old man and walks off, and lies down in the sun, and you go past it to the spring. The Forehead: the second verse is yours.

events.text: The soldier who beat you on the road comes back, sober and grey in the face, with a bucket of windfall chestnuts. He sets it down in the road where he found you that night and backs off, and stands there twisting his cap. "I did not know what you were," he says. "I still do not. I am sorry."

choices.text: Eat the chestnuts in front of him

effects.log: You eat every one, slowly. He watches, and when the bucket is empty he picks it up and goes, and the next autumn he leaves the army and goes home to his father's farm, and he never carries a staff again, not even to walk with.

choices.text: Touch his hand with your nose

effects.log: He goes stiff. Then he puts his other hand on your forehead, on the sore place he made, and keeps it there. He tells the story all his life, in a village a long way off: the night he beat a sacred beast and the morning it forgave him. He tells it badly. He never tells it as anything but his shame.

choices.text: Walk away: it is not something to be paid back

effects.log: You leave the chestnuts and the soldier in the road. Sorry is a thing he must carry, not a thing you can take off him. Behind you, a long time later, you hear him begin to pick up the chestnuts one by one.

events.text: The boys from the wall are young men now. You pass them in the lane, and one of them, the biggest, the one who threw longest, looks at you and goes red to the ears and stops in the middle of the lane. He has a stone in his hand. He is a stonemason. It is a stone for a wall.

choices.text: Stop in front of him and wait

effects.log: He holds the stone. You stand. After a long time he sets it down on the wall, very carefully, as if it might break. "I could not stop," he says, "that day. Because you did not do anything." He goes on down the lane. You stand a little longer. The Forehead: the second verse is yours.

choices.text: Go round him and on to the spring

effects.log: You go round him. He watches you go with the stone in his hand, and afterwards, when he builds walls, he leaves a gap at the bottom of every one, low and narrow, for anything small that needs to get through.

events.text: At the edge of the oak wood, a roe herd: seven of them, red-brown, white-rumped, ears turning like leaves. The old doe at the front looks at you a long time. You are the wrong colour and the wrong shape and you smell of rapids and temple incense. She barks once, the short hoarse bark that means: I see you. Then she turns back to her acorns, and the herd, after her, lets you in.
events.arc: The Roe Deer Who Think You Are One

choices.text: Graze where they graze, on fallen acorns

effects.log: They nose through the leaves for acorns and you nose with them. When they lift their heads, you lift yours. By dark you are a roe deer, more or less, if nobody looks closely. Roe deer do not look closely at each other. It is a great mercy.

choices.text: Stay at the edge and watch how they do it

effects.log: Ears, always, turning. Freeze, then move. Never all heads down at once. You learn more about being a deer in an afternoon than in all your years in the cave. They let you stay at the edge. Roe deer have edges.

choices.text: Bark back to the old doe

effects.log: It comes out wrong, too deep, with something of the temple bell in it. The whole herd lifts its heads. The old doe looks at you for a very long time, and then barks again, softer. You are, it seems, accepted as a peculiar relative.

events.text: A young doe of the herd has decided you are hers. She grazes at your shoulder and sleeps against your flank and follows you down to the spring and back. She is the same age as you, a little smaller, and she does not mind your strangeness at all. At dusk, when the herd barks at shadows, she barks at them twice, once for her and once for you.
events.arc: The Roe Deer Who Think You Are One

choices.text: Let her teach you the dusk bark

effects.log: It is not a warning to the herd, she shows you. It is to the shadow. I see you, it says. So go away, I see you. You learn to say it to foxes and to wolves and once to a woodcutter, who goes away.

choices.text: Teach her to walk on the stones in the rapids

ok.log: She is terrified, and then not, and by the end of summer she can follow you to the big stone in the middle of the white water. She is the only deer on Peony Peak who can. She is very proud of it, in a deer's way, which is to look bored.

fail.log: She goes in up to her neck on the first stone and comes out furious and will not speak to you, in a deer's way, for three days. On the fourth she sleeps against your flank again. Roe deer forgive by forgetting. (-3 health)

choices.text: Sleep a little apart, so she does not get too used to you

effects.log: She comes and lies down against you anyway, every night. You have a feeling about where this goes. You do not have a word for it yet. It is the feeling of a thing that will live a thousand years lying down beside a thing that will live ten.

events.text: A thrum, a hiss, and the young doe at your shoulder goes down in the leaves with an arrow behind the foreleg. The herd explodes in every direction, white rumps flashing. On the ridge a hunter in a straw rain cape is already nocking a second arrow, looking for the rest.
events.arc: The Roe Deer Who Think You Are One

choices.text: Stand over her

effects.log: The second arrow takes you in the flank and bounces off your hide and you do not move. The hunter lowers his bow, staring. She is dead. You stand over her until he comes down the slope, and then you go, because there is nothing to stand over any more. (-10 health)

choices.text: Run with the herd

effects.log: You run with them through the oaks, fast and light, and not a fawn is trampled, because you have learned the way roe deer run, in a scatter, not a crowd. Behind you she is lying in the leaves. You run anyway. That is what the herd does. You were the herd.

choices.text: Charge the hunter on the ridge (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You go up the ridge faster than he can draw and hit him chest-first and he goes down the far side with the bow snapping under him. He gets up limping and runs. You go back to her. It has not made her any less dead. (Bent +3; -6 health)

events.text: You are lying in the reeds by the ford where the hunter's path crosses the stream. He comes down it at dusk with your herd-sister across his shoulders, her head hanging. The bank here is steep and slick. One push, as he steps onto the stones, and he would go into the deep water with her weight on him and not come up.
events.arc: The Roe Deer Who Think You Are One

choices.text: Let him pass

effects.log: He crosses a pace from your nose and never knows. His children will eat this winter. She is still dead. You lie in the reeds until the stars come out, and something in you settles that will be the hardest thing you ever learn, and you learn it here, at a ford, in the reeds.

choices.text: Push him in (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One push. He goes into the deep water with her weight on his shoulders and the current takes them both under the bank. He does not come up. You stand on the bank until the water is smooth. The grass is bent, more than it has ever been bent. (Bent +10)

choices.text: Step out of the reeds and let him see you

ok.log: He stops on the stones. He looks at you, and at the doe on his shoulders, and at you. Then he lays her down on the bank, very gently, as if she were asleep, and backs away up the path, and leaves her. He never hunts on Peony Peak again.

fail.log: He sees you and swears and reaches for an arrow, and has to drop her to do it, and by the time he has the bow up you are gone into the reeds. He picks her up and goes on, looking over his shoulder all the way home. (-4 health)

events.text: The old doe who barked you into the herd is very old now. One morning she does not get up from the leaves. The herd stands round her for a while, ears turning, and then, because they are roe deer, they go on to the acorns. You are bigger than any of them now. Your horn bud has come through. They look at you, waiting.
events.arc: The Roe Deer Who Think You Are One

choices.text: Lead them to the winter acorns

effects.log: You know where they are: the old oaks under the temple, where the monks never gather. The herd follows you. For three winters you are the oldest roe deer on Peony Peak, and the strangest, and they never once ask you why.

choices.text: Stay by the old doe until evening

effects.log: You stand by her all day. The herd comes back at dusk to see if you are coming, and you are, and you go. Nobody should die with nobody there. The monk taught you that without saying it.

choices.text: Leave the herd: you are not a roe deer

effects.log: You stand at the edge of the oak wood and watch them go on without you, white rumps flashing between the trees. You were never a roe deer. You were a roe deer for a while, which is different, and better than nothing.

events.text: At the spring, a grandmother washing radishes is telling her grandchildren an old tale. There is a meadow, she says, high up behind the peak, where the grass springs back up after anything that walks on it. A tiger can cross it and you would not know. An army could. "Only the very lightest thing in the world," she says, "crosses it and leaves the grass happier than it found it."
events.arc: The Meadow That Does Not Bend

choices.text: Go and find the meadow

effects.log: It takes you most of a summer of searching behind the peak. It is there: a long slope of silver grass high up, and when the wind goes over it, it lies down and gets up again like something breathing.

choices.text: Stay and hear the rest of the tale

effects.log: "And what was the lightest thing?" asks the smallest child. "Nobody knows," says the grandmother. "Some say a hare. Some say a sage. My grandmother said it was the thing that lives in the cave under the temple, and that it was not a deer." You go to look for the meadow that night.

events.text: The meadow behind the peak. Long silver grass to your knees, wet with dew, every blade of it standing. You put one hoof in. The grass bows under it, as all grass does. You lift the hoof, and watch, and the grass, very slowly, gets up. You have to cross the whole meadow, and look back, and see nothing.
events.arc: The Meadow That Does Not Bend

choices.text: Cross it, putting every hoof down as if on ice

ok.log: You cross. You look back. The grass stands silver to the edge, dew on every blade but where your hooves were, and even those are rising. It is not nothing. It is very nearly nothing. It is the best thing you have ever done with your feet.

fail.log: You look back and there is a line through the meadow, a dark trail in the dew, slowly lifting. Not broken. Not gone, either. A hare could do it better, you think. You will find out by the end of the week that you are right.

choices.text: Run across it, to see what happens (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You run, because it is a meadow and you are young. At the far side you look back. Most of it is getting up. Here and there, where your hooves came down hard, blades are snapped at the root and will not. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Do not cross: lie at the edge and watch it breathe

effects.log: You lie at the edge all day while the wind goes over the meadow and the grass lies down and gets up, lies down and gets up. By evening you understand that the meadow is not special. All grass does this, if you let it. This is only grass that has been let.

events.text: A brown hare crosses the meadow while you are standing at the edge of it. It does not try. It goes in long unhurried bounds, flop, flop, ears up, and at the far side it sits down and washes its face. Behind it the meadow is exactly as it was. Not a blade lies down. It did not even know there was a test.
events.arc: The Meadow That Does Not Bend

choices.text: Follow the hare, bound for bound

effects.log: You copy it, badly, and then less badly. The trick, it turns out, is not caring. The hare does not think about its feet. It thinks about clover. You think about clover, and cross the meadow, and look back, and there is almost nothing there.

choices.text: Ask the hare how

effects.log: The hare stops washing and looks at you as if you had asked it how to be a hare. Then it goes back to washing. You have your answer. It took you a year to understand it.

events.text: The gorge behind Peony Peak has one way out, a ledge path the width of a cart, and this morning there is an ant road across it. Not a line: a river. Red ants, millions of them, moving house from one side of the gorge to the other, with eggs, with grubs, with soldiers along the edges with their jaws open. It will take all day.

choices.text: Lie down and wait

effects.log: All day. You lie down at the edge of the red river with your chin on your hooves and watch them go. Noon. Afternoon. A soldier ant climbs onto your nose and bites, hard, and you do not move. The sun goes down the gorge. They are still crossing. (-5 health)

choices.text: Jump it

ok.log: A long run on the ledge, a jump that nearly takes you over the edge of the gorge, and you land on the far side with every ant behind you. You are out. It was very fast, and very clever, and you feel, somehow, that you have missed something.

fail.log: You come down a stride short with your back hooves in the edge of the red river. You feel it. They feel it too: a hundred soldiers up your legs, biting. You go on with your legs on fire and the grass bent. (Bent +1; -4 health)

choices.text: Go back and round by the long way, three days

effects.log: Three days over the peak, through thorn, with nothing to eat. You come out on the far side and look down into the gorge, and the ant road is gone, and there is the ledge path, empty. (-6 health)

events.text: Dusk, and the red river is thinning: the last of the grubs, the last soldiers. And then, last of all, slowly, something larger: a queen, winged, as long as your hoof is wide, walking with soldiers all round her. In the middle of the path she stops. She turns. She looks at you, a thing a thousand times her size that has lain in the dust all day for her.

choices.text: Lower your head to her

effects.log: You lower your head until your chin is on the path. She looks at you with her black eyes for as long as it takes the light to change. Then she goes on, into the dark, and the path is yours. You do not know what passed between you. You know something did.

choices.text: Lie still and look back at her

effects.log: Two queens of nothing, looking at each other across a ledge in a gorge. She has a kingdom of millions. You have a cave and a dew bowl. She goes on first. It seems right.

events.text: Every summer after that, wherever you sleep, the ant roads go round it. Not near your head, not under your flank: round, in a neat curve, a pace from you on every side. The monks say the ants know a holy thing. You think the ants know a thing that waited for them all day once, and keep their accounts.

choices.text: Sleep wherever you like, then

effects.log: You sleep in the open meadow, on the ledge path, under the chestnuts, and every morning there is a curve of ants a pace from you. It is the most respectful thing that has ever happened to you, and it was done by ants.

choices.text: Keep moving your bed so their roads stay straight

effects.log: You do not want to be a stone in their river. You sleep somewhere new each night, and the ants stop bending round you, and seem a little disappointed. Even courtesy has to be accepted to be courtesy.

events.text: Lightning on the ridge in a dry autumn, and by midnight the pines above the oak wood are burning. The wind is bringing it down. The whole forest is moving: deer, boar, hares, birds out of the smoke, and in a hollow under a bramble two fawns from a late litter, lying flat as their mother told them, while the fire comes.

choices.text: Carry them out one by one in your mouth

effects.log: By the scruff, as gently as a mouthful of dew, down the slope to the stream and back, through smoke that makes your eyes run. The second one is heavier. You get it out as the bramble catches. Their mother finds them by the stream at dawn and does not understand at all. (-12 health)

choices.text: Run with the rest of the forest (this may bend the grass)

ok.log: You run, and you are light, and you go between the fleeing boar and the fleeing deer without touching any of them. At the stream you turn round. The bramble is burning. You do not know if the fawns are under it. You will never know.

fail.log: You run in the crush of the forest, a boar on one side and a stag on the other, and something small goes under your hooves in the smoke. You never see what. You hear it. (Bent +1; -4 health)

choices.text: Stand in the stream and call them, the way their mother does

ok.log: You bleat the way a roe doe bleats for her young, again and again, until two small spotted shapes come stumbling out of the smoke to the water. You stand over them in the stream all night while the ridge burns.

fail.log: You call until your throat is raw, and they do as their mother told them, and lie flat. In the end you go in and get them, and come out with your face scorched. They live. You are not sure you will look the same. (-6 health)

events.text: The fire has reached the oaks. At the foot of the biggest one there is a badger sett, and in the mouth of it the old badger is standing, fur on end, refusing. Its family is down there. It will not leave them, and they will not come out into the smoke.

choices.text: Go into the smoke and drag the old badger away

ok.log: It bites you twice. You drag it anyway, by the scruff, out of the sett mouth and down to the stream, and the family, hearing it scream, come boiling up out of the earth after it. All of them. The oak burns. (-15 health)

fail.log: The smoke comes down over the sett mouth like a lid. You get the badger by the scruff and lose it and lose the way, and come out on the wrong side of the oak with your coat smoking. The badgers are not there. Neither, nearly, are you. (-20 health)
fail.deathCause: the fire on Peony Peak, going back for a badger

choices.text: Stand in the sett mouth so the badger has to go round you

effects.log: It cannot hold the sett mouth with you in it. It goes down into the earth, cursing, and you lie across the entrance with the fire going over the top of the oak, and the earth keeps them. In the morning they come out under you, singed and alive. (-8 health)

choices.text: Leave them: the earth is the best place in a fire

effects.log: You go. Badgers have lived through fires in the earth since before there were deer. In the spring you see the old badger on the burned slope, nosing in the ash, and it does not look at you at all.

events.text: In the worst of it, coming back through the burning bramble for the second fawn, you looked down and saw your legs on fire. Pale fire, almost white, curling round your knees and hooves. You did not stop. You did not burn. Now, in the cold ash by the stream at dawn, you look at your legs. Nothing. Only unburnt hide. Under your hooves the ash has not even been disturbed.

choices.text: Look for the fire again

effects.log: It does not come when you look for it. It came when you went back into a fire for something smaller than you. You will find, over many centuries, that this is the only way it ever comes.

choices.text: Step on a live coal to see

effects.log: It burns. Your hoof is still soft. Whatever the pale fire was, it was not for you. You lick your hoof and think about that for a long time. (-3 health)

events.text: Two springs after the fire the burned ridge is green again, the way the monks said it would be: bracken first, then bush clover, then the oaks coming up from their roots as if nothing had happened. Two young roe deer are grazing on it, still a little spotted at the hips. They look up at you and do not run.

choices.text: Graze beside them

effects.log: They do not know you. They know you a little. You stand in the new bracken with the two fawns you brought out of a fire, all three of you eating fallen things, and nobody says anything, because deer do not.

choices.text: Walk the whole burned ridge, and count what came back

effects.log: Bracken. Clover. Oak. A fox den. The badgers. Not the old pines: those will take a hundred years. You will be here in a hundred years. You make a note to come and see.

events.text: Hungry. Real hunger, the kind that makes the world go thin at the edges. The meadow below the cave is green and new, and the new grass smells of everything good, and every animal in the valley is eating it. You put your mouth down to it. And stop. Something in you will not close its teeth on a thing that is growing.

choices.text: Eat it anyway: you are hungry (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: It is sweet and green and wrong, all at once. You eat a whole patch, and the hunger goes, and something else comes in its place and stays much longer. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Lick the dew off it instead

effects.log: A drop from every blade, a thousand blades, and the grass stands up again behind your tongue a little lighter. It is not enough to live on. It is enough to start with.

choices.text: Eat the dead leaves under the hedge

effects.log: Brown, bitter, a year old. They are not growing. You eat them. They taste of patience and a little of mould. It is the beginning of a long, odd diet.

events.text: Autumn, and the old chestnut trees on the ridge are dropping their spiked husks. Under them, the squirrels, and a boy from the village with a long pole, knocking the husks down. The ones he knocks down are falling. The ones that fell in the night have already fallen. You stand at the edge of the trees, working out a rule.

choices.text: Eat only what fell by itself in the night

effects.log: You are at the trees before dawn every morning, before the boy and the pole. What the tree let go of, you take. What the boy shakes out of it, you leave for the boy. It seems fair. The squirrels think it is mad.

choices.text: Eat what the boy knocks down: it has fallen, after all

effects.log: It has fallen. You were not the pole. The boy sees you eating his chestnuts and throws his pole and runs, and you eat all of them, and it is a fine autumn, and you are not sure, at all, about the rule.

choices.text: Leave the chestnuts to the squirrels and the boy

effects.log: You eat windfall acorns under the oaks instead, which are bitter, and which nobody wants. The squirrels watch you go with deep suspicion. Generosity, to a squirrel, is the act of a lunatic. (-2 health)

events.text: A hard winter, and nothing has fallen. The chestnuts are gone, the acorns are gone, the dead leaves are under three feet of snow, and the dew is ice. You are thin enough that the roe deer look at you sideways. The bark of the young ash by the stream is green under the snow, and smells of spring.

choices.text: Dig under the snow for last year's acorns

effects.log: Hours of digging for a mouthful. Then another hour for another. You find enough to stay alive, and not one acorn more. You dig with your soft hooves until they bleed. (-6 health)

choices.text: Strip the bark of the young ash (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: It is green and bitter and it keeps you alive. In the spring the young ash does not leaf. You walk past it every day for a year, a grey stick by the stream. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Go up to the temple and stand at the kitchen door

ok.log: A kitchen monk with a ladle opens the door and nearly drops it. Then the monk sets down the rice scrapings that would have gone to the birds, and goes in, and comes out again with more. All winter. The temple record says only: a hard winter; we fed the deer.

fail.log: The kitchen monk takes you for a thief deer and chases you off with a ladle. You go back down to the snow and dig. (-4 health)

events.text: The thaw. The first things to fall, before anything has grown: plum petals off the old tree by the temple wall, white and thin, on the wet stones. Nothing has died to make them. The tree let them go. You stand under it at dawn with petals coming down on your back.

choices.text: Eat the petals off the stones

effects.log: They taste of almost nothing, cold and faintly sweet. It is the first meal of the year that was given to you entirely, by something that did not mind giving it. You will eat fallen petals every spring for a thousand years.

choices.text: Stand under the tree and let them fall on you

effects.log: A young monk crossing the court sees a grey deer under the plum tree, white with petals, eyes closed. He stops sweeping. He forgets, for the rest of the morning, what he was sweeping for.

events.text: Down the river from the temple there is a horse pasture of the royal stables, with long thatched sheds and a horse-master who shouts. A child of the stables, {npc}, small and patched and smelling of hay, finds you at the pasture fence one morning and decides you are a strange colt that has got loose. {He} has a rope halter, plaited {him}self, and a handful of hay.

choices.text: Let {him} put the halter on

effects.log: The halter goes round your head. {npc} is so pleased {he} hops. You stand there, haltered, while {he} explains to you at length about the horse-master, and the ponies, and which pony bites. You do not eat the hay. {He} does not notice.

choices.text: Back away, but slowly

effects.log: {npc} follows, with the halter held out, talking to you in the voice for frightened colts. You keep a pace ahead. It goes on all morning, across the whole pasture. By noon you are, without anyone deciding it, friends.

choices.text: Take the hay, then go

effects.log: It is cut hay, already dead. You take it from {his} hand. {npc} laughs out loud. You go off up the river with hay in your mouth, and {he} shouts after you that {he} will bring more tomorrow, and {he} does.

events.text: {npc} has brought a bridle. A real one, from the tack room, iron bit and leather, too big for {his} arms. {He} holds it up to you, very serious. "If you wear this," {he} says, "the horse-master will let you stay. You can live in the stables. I will look after you. Every day."

choices.text: Open your mouth for the bit

effects.log: The iron is cold and tastes of other mouths. {npc} buckles it with great care, wrong, and leads you round the pasture once, beaming. The ponies stare. You let {him}. You wear it until dusk, and then you work it off against a fence post, and leave it hanging there neatly. (-4 health)

choices.text: Shake your head, gently

effects.log: {npc} tries again. You shake your head again. {He} puts the bridle down and sits on it and cries a little, and then stops, and says, "You are not a horse, are you." It is not a question. You stand beside {him} until {he} has finished thinking it.

choices.text: Take the bridle in your teeth and carry it back to the tack room

ok.log: You walk into the tack room with it hanging from your mouth and hang it on its peg, more or less. {npc} follows, open-mouthed. When the horse-master counts the bridles that night, they are all there. {npc} keeps the secret all {his} life.

fail.log: The horse-master is in the tack room. You see each other at the same time. The horse-master roars, and you drop the bridle and go out through the far wall, which is only woven straw. {npc} gets the blame and a cuffing, and laughs about it for years. (-3 health)

events.text: The horse-master has seen you at last. The man comes down the pasture with three grooms and a coil of rope and a long whip, the kind for breaking colts, and {npc} running behind, pulling at the man's sleeve. "A colt like that," the horse-master says, "is worth a governor's favour. Broken, it is."

choices.text: Stand and let them come, and do not fight

effects.log: The rope goes over your neck. The whip comes down, once, twice. You do not answer it. Then {npc} throws {him}self between you and the whip, and the horse-master stops with the whip raised, and in that moment you step out of the rope as if it were not there, and you are gone up the river. (-10 health)

choices.text: Run before they reach you

effects.log: Up the river, onto the stones in the rapids, and the grooms stop at the water. The horse-master swears. {npc}, at the back, is laughing so hard {he} has to sit down in the mud.

choices.text: Kick the horse-master when the rope comes (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your hoof takes the horse-master in the knee, and the man goes down screaming. The grooms drop the rope. You go. Behind you {npc} stands in the pasture looking from the horse-master on the ground to you, going away, and you see {his} face. It is the face of someone who has just found out what a thing is. (Bent +3)

events.text: {npc} is grown, a groom of the royal stables now, with a groom's bandy walk. {He} finds you at the river at dawn, as {he} has found you a hundred times. Today the light falls on your forehead, and {he} sees the horn bud that has come through, and stops dead, and goes white. "Oh," {he} says. "Oh. You are the other thing."

choices.text: Lower your head so {he} can touch it

effects.log: {He} puts out a hand that is shaking and touches the bud with one fingertip. It is soft. {npc} laughs and cries at once. "I tried to put a bit in your mouth," {he} says. "I tried to put a bit in your mouth." {He} cannot stop saying it.

choices.text: Stand still and let {him} understand in {his} own time

effects.log: It takes {him} a long time. Every year {he} spent with you goes past behind {his} eyes, the halter, the hay, the bridle held up. Then {he} sits down on the bank. "Well," {he} says. "That explains the hay."

choices.text: Go, before {he} has to decide what to do

effects.log: You turn and go up the river. You do not see {npc} again for a long time. When you do, {he} is the horse-master, and there is a rule in the royal stables, which nobody understands, that no colt is ever broken with a whip.

events.text: You come home through the rain and there is a fire in your cave. Six men round it, with spears and a stolen ox, and they have pulled your straw into a heap to sleep on. They are laughing about a village they left burning. Above the cave mouth, on the cliff edge, there is a boulder you have always walked round, because it moves when the wind is strong.

choices.text: Go out into the rain and leave them the cave

effects.log: You stand under a pine in the rain all night with water running off your coat. In the morning they are still there, sleeping off the ox. The straw is ruined and the hollow has a fire-pit in it. You do not care. Nobody is under the boulder. (-6 health)

choices.text: Push the boulder down onto the cave mouth (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: It goes at the third push. The noise is the end of the world. When the rain has washed the dust away, the cave mouth is half shut, and nothing in it is laughing. You did it for a burned village. The grass does not know why. It only knows. (Bent +10)

choices.text: Go in and stand in the firelight until they see you

ok.log: One of them looks up and screams, and then all of them are on their feet with spears out, staring at a scaled thing in the cave mouth that does not move. The youngest drops his spear first. They leave the ox. They leave everything. They go out into the rain without a word, and they never come back to Peony Peak.

fail.log: A spear comes out of the firelight and opens your shoulder before anyone has thought. You go back out into the rain and they stay, laughing louder, and you hear them all night. (-10 health)

events.text: The bandits are still in your cave on the second night, and they have found the old hoof-hollows in the straw and the great prints on the stone outside. One of them, a thin one with a scholar's hands, is on his knees by the Morning-Heaven Stone with a torch, very quiet. "I know what lives here," he says to the others. "If we wait, it comes back. If we take it, we never rob again."

choices.text: Do not come back: let them wait for nothing

effects.log: They wait three nights. You sleep in the oaks. On the fourth morning the others make the thin one leave, and he goes last, looking back at the stone. You think he will come back. You think he will be sorry when he does.

choices.text: Show yourself on the far bank, once, and lead them away

ok.log: They come after you down the slope and across the meadow and into the oak wood, and you lose them in the dusk, and they never find the way back to the cave. The thin one dreams about it all his life.

fail.log: They are quicker than you thought. A thrown net catches your hind legs on the meadow and you tear out of it, bleeding. Now they know it is real. (-8 health)

events.text: Years later, a beggar with a scholar's hands comes up the goat track to the cave on his knees. He has no spear. He sits on the Morning-Heaven Stone, a long way from you, and says: "I wanted to catch you. To stop robbing, I said. I never stopped. Now I am old, and I only want to see you once before I die."

choices.text: Come out and let him see you

effects.log: You come out of the cave and stand on the stone at arm's length. He looks for a long time. He does not reach for you. Then he goes down the track, slowly, and in the village below he gives the last of what he stole to the temple, and sweeps its steps until he dies.

choices.text: Stay hidden: you do not owe him that

effects.log: He sits on the stone until dark and goes away without seeing you. You did not owe him. You think about it for a long time afterwards, whether that is the same as being right.

events.text: Your forehead itches. Not the itch of a fly or a burr: an itch from inside, in the bone, in one place, right in the middle, the place everything seems to hit. You rub it on every tree on Peony Peak. In the still pool under the rapids you look at yourself, and there, under the coat, there is a bump. One. Soft.

choices.text: Rub it on the old pine until it stops

effects.log: It does not stop. The pine gets a smooth place on its bark the height of your forehead, and it keeps it for two hundred years, and the woodcutters call it the deer's pine and leave it standing. (-2 health)

choices.text: Look at it in the pool for a long time

effects.log: One. Not two, like the stags. One, in the middle, soft. Whatever you are, you are not a deer. You had suspected it. Now there is a bump to prove it.

choices.text: Leave it alone and let it come

effects.log: You stop rubbing. It comes anyway, slowly, the way the grass gets up. By the end of the year there is a small soft rounded thing on your forehead that is very definitely the beginning of a horn, and that, when you touch it to your foreleg, is warm.

events.text: Two young monks are arguing on the temple steps over an old book, and you are listening from the ferns. "It is a qi," says one. "The qi has the horn." "It is a lin," says the other. "The lin has the horn. The qi has none." "Then which is the one with the soft end?" They both look at the book. The book, being a book, does not say.

choices.text: Walk out and show them the horn

effects.log: They look at you. They look at the horn. They look at the book. "Well," says the first. "It is a qilin," says the second, very quietly, and shuts the book. The books can argue. You go back to the ferns.

choices.text: Leave them arguing

effects.log: They argue until the bell. You walk away thinking that you are something two books disagree about, and that this is probably how it will always be, and that you do not mind. You are a qilin. The books can argue.

events.text: A fox on the rock by the cave mouth when you come back from the meadow. Red, sharp, smiling, and with three tails, which it arranges round itself as if they were a perfectly ordinary number of tails. "So you are the foal," it says, in a voice like honey on a knife. "I expected something prettier. You walk like a crane with sore feet."

choices.text: Say nothing and walk past

effects.log: "Oh, good," says the fox behind you. "A silent one. I love the silent ones. They take longer." You do not know what it means. You know you will find out.

choices.text: Answer it politely

effects.log: "Good morning," you say. The fox laughs till its three tails shake. "Good morning," it says. "Good morning! Oh, you are going to be such fun." It is gone before you see it go.

choices.text: Ask why it has three tails

effects.log: "Because I have been very patient," says the fox. "One day I will have nine. And you? What will you have, in a thousand years, little crane-foot? Nothing. Nothing on your forehead but a lump." It grins. It seems to know things.

events.text: The fox again, on the path, every few days. It says things. Whatever left you in the straw left because you were ugly. The monks laugh at you. The roe deer only pretend. Today it walks up close, sweet as a cat, and while you are listening it darts in and bites your ear, hard enough to bleed, and sits back to see what you will do.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let your ear bleed

effects.log: You stand there with blood running down your neck. The fox waits. And waits. Then it yawns, extravagantly. "Dull," it says. "Dull, dull." But its eyes are not bored at all. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stamp at it so it jumps back
