effects.log: It jumps back, delighted. "There!" it says. "There it is! A little temper!" You did not touch it. It does not care. It saw what it wanted: the start of a kick. (-4 health)

choices.text: Catch it by the tail and throw it in the rapids (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You catch a tail, one of the three, and swing, and it goes out over the white water and in, and comes out far downstream, soaked, limping, and laughing. "Yes!" it calls across the river. "Yes, yes, YES!" You stand on the bank and feel sick. (Bent +3; -4 health)

events.text: The dew bowl. The monk set it down at dawn as always, and before you get there the fox has lapped it up, every drop, and is sitting beside it licking its lips. It upends the bowl with one paw so it rolls off the stone and cracks. "Oops," says the fox.

choices.text: Pick up the pieces and set them on the step for the monk

effects.log: You carry the two halves of the bowl to the bottom step one at a time. The fox watches with its head on one side. "You are going to be very boring for a very long time," it says, and for the first time it does not sound pleased about it.

choices.text: Go without, and walk away

effects.log: You go down to the meadow and lick the dew off the grass instead. The fox follows, all the way, talking. You do not answer once. That evening, for the first time, it leaves before you do. (-3 health)

choices.text: Chase it off the stone, butting (this may bend the grass)

ok.log: You go at it with your head down and it is gone before your head arrives, and sits on a higher rock, grinning. "Close," it says. "So close." You did not touch it. You meant to. You know you meant to, and so does it.

fail.log: You catch it this time. Your forehead takes it in the ribs and something cracks and it rolls off the stone and lies there, laughing through its teeth, holding its side. "There," it says. "Now we both know." (Bent +3)

events.text: The fox comes at dusk and lies down on the Morning-Heaven Stone with its three tails over the great hoofprints, as if they were a bed made for it. It puts its chin on its paws in the largest print, the one you put your hoof in. It looks at you. It is waiting, very patiently, for you to be angry.

choices.text: Lie down on the other side of the stone

effects.log: You lie down, a pace from it, and put your own chin on your hooves. You both lie there as the stars come out. "Why," says the fox at last, quite quietly. "Why will you not." You do not know how to say it. It does not need you to. It goes, and does not take its time about going.

choices.text: Ask it to get off

effects.log: "No," says the fox, and smiles. You stand there. It stays there. In the end you go and sleep in the cave. In the morning it is gone and there are three neat paw-marks of mud in the print, as if to say: mine too, now.

choices.text: Push it off the stone (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your shoulder sends it off the stone and down the slope in a tumble of tails. It is not hurt. It is not hurt at all. It sits up at the bottom of the slope and laughs for a long time, and you know it has learned something about you that you did not want it to know. (Bent +1)

events.text: The fox is leaving Peony Peak. It tells you so, sitting on the rock where you first met it, washing one of its three tails with great care. "There is a king in the south," it says, "with a very interesting son. I will be back when I have more tails." It looks at you. "And when you have a horn. I want to see what you do with it."

choices.text: Tell it: nothing

effects.log: "Nothing," you say. The fox laughs. "Everyone says nothing," it says, "until someone they love is under a sword." It goes down the goat track, three tails swinging. You will see it again. It has promised, and it is the kind of creature that keeps only that kind of promise.

choices.text: Wish it well, honestly

effects.log: "Go well," you say, and mean it. The fox stops in the track. It looks back at you for a long time, and something goes across its face that it puts away very quickly. "You are a dangerous thing," it says. "Do you know that?" Then it is gone.

events.text: Before dawn, in the dark, the bell of the temple above the cave speaks. One stroke. It goes through the rock and into the straw and into your ribs, and the whole cave hums with it. Then another, and another. You count, without knowing that you are counting. Twenty-eight. Then silence, and the drum begins.

choices.text: Lie still and feel it in your ribs

effects.log: Twenty-eight strokes, every dawn, and every one of them goes through you as if you were part of the bell. By the end of the season you wake a breath before the first stroke, and lie there, waiting for it, like waiting for someone you love.

choices.text: Answer it

effects.log: You do not know what sound you make. A foal's sound, thin, with something else in it. Up in the bell pavilion, the monk on the striker misses the twenty-ninth stroke, which there was never meant to be, and stands with the beam swinging, listening.

events.text: You answer the bell every dawn now. And this morning, when the last stroke dies away and you answer it, the drum does not start. The wooden fish does not start. Up on the cliff, every monk in the temple has stopped, mallets in the air, listening to the sound coming up from the cave below the temple, because it is the same note as the bell.

choices.text: Keep the note as long as you can

ok.log: You hold it until your ribs ache, and the bell, which is still humming, hums with you, and for a moment there is one sound in the valley and two things making it. Then the drum begins, late, very gently, as if apologising.

fail.log: Your voice cracks halfway like a young cockerel's. Up on the cliff someone laughs, and is hushed. The drum starts. But they heard the first half. They heard what it was.

choices.text: Stop, embarrassed

effects.log: You stop. The silence goes on a long time. Then the drum starts, and the fish, and the cloud gong for the creatures of the air, and the service goes on as if nothing had happened. But the next morning, you notice, they strike the bell a little more slowly, as if leaving room.

events.text: The young monk who strikes the bell has started coming down to the cave mouth after the dawn service and sitting on the stone, out of breath from the steps. "The drum is for the beasts that walk," he tells you, as if you had asked. "The wooden fish for what swims. The cloud gong for what flies. The bell for everything else. I always wondered which one was for you. Now I think it is the bell."

choices.text: Hum the bell note for him, quietly

effects.log: He closes his eyes. When you stop he sits there a long time. "Yes," he says. "That is the one." From then on he strikes the bell differently, and the old monks say he has finally got the hang of it, and he never tells them why.

choices.text: Listen to him explain the rest

effects.log: He tells you the whole service: the bell, then the drum, then the fish, then the gong, so that everything that lives hears something. For a creature that wants to harm nothing, it is good to know that every morning, somebody rings for all of them.

events.text: Spring thaw, and the rapids have come up over the stones and over the bank and over the ferry road. The ferry below the temple has broken its rope. You see it from the bank: the boat turning over, the ferryman swimming, and a child, {npc}, holding the end of the broken rope in the brown water, going round in the eddy below the big stone.

choices.text: Go out on the stones you know, under the flood

ok.log: Every stone is under the water, but you know where they are. Stone, stone, and the big stone, and then there is no stone and you go on anyway, and for one step, two, the flood holds you up. You get your teeth in the child's jacket and turn for the bank. Nobody on the bank says a word.

fail.log: The second stone is not there. You go under in the brown water and the flood throws you against the big stone and holds you there. You come up with the child against your chest somehow and are thrown out on the bank a li downstream, both of you, alive, barely. (-20 health)
fail.deathCause: the spring flood on the White Silver Rapids

choices.text: Run down the bank and push a log out to {him}

effects.log: A drift log at the water's edge. You shove it out with your head and shoulders into the eddy and {npc} lets go of the rope and grabs it, and the log and {npc} come round to the shallows. You stand in the cold to your chest until {he} is out. (-6 health)

choices.text: Bark, loud, until the people on the far bank see

effects.log: You bark the roe bark, over and over, at the far bank, until a man there sees what you are barking at and runs for a rope. {npc} is pulled out half drowned. Nobody looks at you. They were looking at the child.

events.text: {npc}, the ferry child, has told the whole village that a deer was there in the flood and saved {him}. Nobody believes it. The ferryman, who was swimming at the time, says it was a log. {npc} comes up to the bank below the cave every evening and calls into the rapids: "I know you were there."

choices.text: Come down to the bank and let {him} see you

mem.note: came down to the bank, so I knew

effects.log: You come down out of the ferns. {npc} goes very still, and then grins, the grin of someone who has been right in front of the whole village and will now go on being right for the rest of {his} life. {He} does not run to tell anyone. {He} sits with you until dark.

choices.text: Stay in the ferns: it does not matter who believes

effects.log: {npc} calls every evening for a month and then stops. {He} still knows. Knowing alone, you think, is a thing worth learning young. You are learning it too.

events.text: The flood has gone down and you go back to the rapids and stand where the big stone is, and then step off it, onto the water, the way you did with the child in your teeth. You go straight in up to your shoulders.

choices.text: Try again, and again

effects.log: All summer you step off the big stone into the water, and all summer the water takes you. It held you once, when you were not thinking about yourself at all. You suspect that is the whole trick, and that you cannot learn it on purpose. (-4 health)

choices.text: Let it be: it was for the child, not for you

effects.log: You stand on the big stone and do not step off. The water held you for one breath because a child was drowning. It will hold you again, one day, for good. You can wait. You are very good at waiting.

events.text: {npc} is the ferryman now. When {he} poles the ferry past the big stone in the rapids {he} lifts the pole out of the water and holds it up, every time, like a salute. The passengers think it is a ferryman's luck charm. {npc} lets them. Today, as {he} passes, you are standing on the big stone.

choices.text: Lift your head to {him}

mem.note: lifted your head to me from the stone

effects.log: {npc} nearly drops the pole. Every passenger on the ferry sees you. Half of them say afterwards it was a deer. The other half say nothing at all, which in that valley is how you can tell they believed.

choices.text: Step down behind the stone before the passengers see

effects.log: Only {npc} sees you go. {He} smiles and lifts the pole, as always. The passengers ask what the charm is for. "For the stone," says {npc}. "It is a lucky stone." It is, now.

events.text: A charcoal kiln at the edge of the oak wood, an earth mound with blue smoke leaking from it, and a child with a black face sitting on a log to watch the smoke, as the charcoal-maker has told {him} to. {npc} looks up from the smoke and sees you between the oaks, grey-gold, with the bud of a horn. {He} does not run. {He} does not shout. {He} only looks.

choices.text: Stand and let {him} look

mem.note: let me see you at the kiln

effects.log: You stand. {npc} looks. It goes on until the smoke changes colour and the charcoal-maker shouts from the hut, and {npc} turns round for one breath, and when {he} turns back the oaks are empty. {He} has seen something. {He} will never be able to prove it.

choices.text: Step back into the trees

effects.log: You go. But {npc} saw. It does not take long to see a thing like you, only a breath, and that breath is in {him} now for good.

choices.text: Come closer, very slowly

ok.log: Close enough to smell the charcoal on {him}. {npc} puts out a black hand, and you let it touch your neck, and it leaves a mark of soot on your coat you carry home and are strangely sorry to wash off.

fail.log: A twig cracks under your hoof, the only twig you have cracked in a year, and the charcoal-maker comes out of the hut with a stick, and you are gone. {npc} saw. That is enough. It will turn out to be too much.

events.text: {npc} has told the village. A scaled deer with one horn, at the kiln. The old women know what that is. They say it in whispers in the well lane, then out loud in the market: a sage is coming. A great one. In this village. Somebody's baby. Every woman with child in three villages is suddenly very interesting, and {npc} is a hero.

choices.text: Stay away: you are not here for a sage

effects.log: You keep to the far side of the peak all year. No sage comes. Babies are born, ordinary babies, red and loud. The village waits, and then it stops waiting, and then it begins to look at {npc}.

choices.text: Go and look at the babies, to see

effects.log: You stand at the edge of the village at dusk while a baby is born in a house by the well. Nothing in you moves. It is a baby. It is a good baby. It is not what they hoped. You go back up the peak, and you do not know yet that one day you will feel the other thing, and know it at once.

events.text: No sage came. Years of no sage. And now {npc}, the charcoal-maker's child, is the joke of three villages: the child who saw a holy beast at a kiln. Children bleat at {him} in the lane. A grown man asks {him}, in the market, in front of everyone, if {he} has seen any dragons lately. {npc} has stopped saying it was real. {He} has not stopped knowing.

choices.text: Go back to the kiln, once, so {he} knows

mem.note: came back to the kiln so I would know

effects.log: Dusk, the kiln smoking, {npc} on the log, older and thinner. You come out of the oaks and stand where you stood before. {He} sees you. {He} does not run to tell anyone, ever again. {He} only nods, once, the way you nod to a friend across a market. It is enough to live on. It is enough for {his} whole life.

choices.text: Stay away: going back would only start it all again

effects.log: You think it through and stay away. It would start again. They would laugh harder. You are probably right. On the far side of the peak, you are not sure that probably is enough.

choices.text: Show yourself to the whole market, to prove {him} right

ok.log: You walk down the middle of the market at noon. Every stall stops. The man who asked about dragons drops a basket of eggs. {npc} stands by the well with {his} mouth open, and then, slowly, begins to laugh, and does not stop for a very long time.

fail.log: You get halfway down the market before someone throws a net from a stall. You tear free and go, but now the whole province has heard there is something worth netting on Peony Peak. {npc} watches you go. {He} is not laughed at any more. {He} is asked, by hard men, where the kiln is. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc} keeps the kiln now, a charcoal-maker with a black face and a child of {his} own on the log to watch the smoke. You hear {him} telling the child, one evening, the story of the scaled deer at the kiln. {He} tells it plainly. {He} does not say a sage was coming. {He} says: "It came back, so I would know. That is all. It came back."

choices.text: Let the child see you too

effects.log: The small one on the log looks up and sees you between the oaks. {npc} does not turn round. {He} smiles at the smoke. "Yes," {he} says. "Like that."

choices.text: Listen to the end and go

effects.log: It is a short story, the way {npc} tells it. No sage. No omen. A child and a beast and a kiln, and the beast came back. You have been told about in many ways since. That one is still your favourite.

events.text: On the cliff path above the gorge, in the half-light, something closes round your foreleg and pulls tight. A snare. Not hemp: silk, fine and grey, strong as wire, tied to a pine root. Somebody knew what they were setting it for. The more you pull, the deeper it goes into the soft place above the hoof.

choices.text: Stand still and wait for whoever comes

effects.log: You stop pulling. It stops cutting. You stand on three legs with the fourth held out by a grey thread, at the edge of a drop, and wait, and the sun comes up, and someone is coming up the path. (-6 health)

choices.text: Pull until something gives

ok.log: The pine root gives before the silk does. You go down the path dragging a root on a grey thread and lie up in the ferns and work the noose off with your teeth all day. The leg will carry the scar for two hundred years. (-12 health)

fail.log: The silk does not give. The root does not give. Your leg does, a little, at the soft place. You stand shaking on three legs at the edge of the drop, bleeding into the moss, and someone is coming up the path. (-14 health)

choices.text: Chew through the cord

ok.log: Silk is strong. Your teeth are patient. It takes until the sun is high, and you are gone before anyone comes up the path. You leave the cut end hanging from the root, neat, for the snare-setter to find and think about. (-4 health)

fail.log: Your teeth slide on the silk, and every time you bend to it the noose bites deeper. Someone is coming up the path, whistling. (-8 health)

events.text: The snare-setter comes up the path with a sack and a knife: {npc}, lean and quick, with the eyes of someone who has heard what the horn of a five-coloured beast fetches from the alchemists in the city. {He} stops when {he} sees you. Then {he} smiles and comes on. {He} is standing on the very edge of the cliff path, between you and the drop.

choices.text: Stand and look at {him}

effects.log: {npc} stops a pace away with the knife out. You look at {him}. {He} looks at you. The knife wavers, the way the boys' stones did, the way the soldier's staff did. You are learning what it is about you that does that. It is that you are not going to do anything.

choices.text: Kick {him} off the cliff (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One kick with your free hind leg. {npc} goes off the edge of the path without a sound and the gorge takes {him}. You stand alone in the snare on the empty path. Nobody is coming to cut you free now. Nobody is coming at all. The grass is bent, far and deep. (Bent +10)

choices.text: Lower your head and show {him} the horn bud

ok.log: {npc} sees the horn and the soft end of it and goes white. "It is only a bud," {he} says, to {him}self. "It is only a bud. They pay for the whole horn." {He} backs off down the path, still talking to {him}self, and stops at the bend to wait, for you to grow or for you to weaken. You have bought time. Not much.

fail.log: {npc} sees the horn and laughs. "A bud!" {he} says. "Better. Young horn, young blood." {He} comes on with the knife, and is reaching for your head, when an old voice on the path behind {him} clears its throat. (-8 health)

events.text: Up the cliff path, behind the snare-setter, comes a grandmother with a white headscarf, a basket of bracken on the back and a sickle in the belt. The old woman looks at the snare-setter, and the knife, and you on three legs in the silk. Not a word to {npc}. The sickle comes out of the belt and the old woman comes past {him} as if {he} were a pine stump, and bends to your foreleg.

choices.text: Hold still for the sickle

effects.log: The sickle goes in under the silk, flat, against your leg, and twists, and the noose falls in the moss. The old woman wraps your leg in a strip of the white headscarf. "There. Go on." {npc} says that is a fortune walking away. "Then it is a fortune," says the grandmother, "that walks." You go.

choices.text: Look at the snare-setter while the sickle cuts

effects.log: You look at {npc} the whole time. {He} cannot look at you, or at the grandmother, or at anything. When the silk falls {he} picks it up out of the moss, without thinking, and stands holding it, a grey thread, worth nothing now.

events.text: Years later, the snare-setter again: older, poorer, with a cough, and a new silk snare across the deer path below the temple. You see it before it sees you. {npc} is sitting on a rock above it, waiting. Then {he} sees you, standing on the far side of the snare, looking at {him}, and for a long moment neither of you moves.

choices.text: Pull the snare loose with your teeth while {he} watches

mem.note: pulled my snare loose in front of me

effects.log: You take the cord in your teeth and pull it off its root and drop it at {his} feet. {npc} picks it up. {He} turns it over in {his} hands. "I am too old for this," {he} says at last, to the snare. {He} winds it up and puts it in {his} jacket and goes, coughing.

choices.text: Walk round it and on, and let {him} see you do it

effects.log: You go round it. {npc} watches you go, and then comes down off the rock and stands looking at the empty snare a long time. The next spring there are no snares on the deer path. The spring after, there is one, and the year after that, none.

choices.text: Lie down on the deer path in front of the snare, so nothing walks into it

effects.log: You lie down across the path. Nothing comes past you into the snare, all day. {npc} sits on the rock all day. At dusk {he} comes down and takes the snare up, and does not look at you, and goes home. (-4 health)

events.text: The grandmother with the sickle is very old now. You find her house by the white cloth hung on her gate to dry: the same weave as the strip she bound your leg with. She is sitting in the sun on the step, too old for the bracken slopes, shelling beans, and she looks up and sees you at the gate.

choices.text: Come in through the gate

effects.log: She does not get up. She holds out a bean pod, as if to a calf. You do not eat it. She laughs. "Still fussy," she says. "I thought so." You lie down by the step in the sun while she shells, and her grandchildren come out and see you, and are told it is a deer, and are not fooled.

choices.text: Stand at the gate and lower your head

effects.log: She looks at you for a long time. "It was nothing," she says. "A sickle." You stay at the gate until she goes in. When she dies, that winter, her family finds a heap of windfall chestnuts on the step, every morning for a week, and nobody knows who brought them.

events.text: The grandmother has gone down the path with her bracken. The snare-setter is still standing there with the cut silk in {his} hand, and {he} laughs, a short ugly laugh. "It was always like this," {he} says. "My grandfather threw a stone at one, once, when he was a boy. A stone. It stopped in the air in front of the beast and fell in the dust, and not a blade bent, he said. He spent his whole life telling it. I wanted to be the one who did more than throw a stone."

choices.text: Look at {him} until {he} stops laughing

effects.log: A stone stopped in the air, long ago, in some other life, and a child never forgot it. You do not remember the stone. Something in you does. {npc} stops laughing. {He} drops the silk in the moss and walks away down the path, and you think, for the first time, that a thing can come down a family like a debt.

choices.text: Go down the path and leave {him} to it

effects.log: You go down the path on four legs. Behind you {npc} is still talking about {his} grandfather and the stone. Some families keep the wrong half of a story for a hundred years.

events.text: Night, and you are crossing the meadow to the stream in the dark, and the dark is full of frogs. It rained at dusk. They are everywhere, out on the wet grass, singing, and you cannot see them, only hear them, all round your hooves.

choices.text: Go on slowly, feeling for each step

ok.log: Toe first, weight after, every step a question. It takes an hour to cross a meadow you could run in a breath. You reach the stream with not one frog the quieter. They sing you all the way there.

fail.log: Halfway across, under your hind hoof, a frog stops singing. Only one, among hundreds. Nobody notices but you. You stand very still for a long time. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Wait for the moon

effects.log: You lie down at the edge of the meadow and wait for the moon to rise, thirsty, while the frogs sing. When it comes up you can see every one of them. You cross, picking your way, and drink. (-2 health)

choices.text: Go round by the stony ridge instead

effects.log: Twice as far, on sharp stones, in the dark. You bark your shins. Not one frog. (-3 health)

events.text: A fledgling sparrow has fallen out of its nest into the leaf litter right where you are about to put your hoof. It is too small to fly and too stupid to hide, and it opens its whole beak at you and shrieks, as if you were its mother with a worm.

choices.text: Lift it back into the nest

ok.log: You stand on your hind legs against the trunk with the fledgling in your soft lips and tip it into the nest, where it shrieks at its brothers instead. The mother sparrow comes back and is very rude to you for no reason at all.

fail.log: You cannot reach. You lay it in a fork of the roots out of the path and stand guard until the mother comes down and finds it. It is something. It is not the nest.

choices.text: Step round it and go on

effects.log: You go round. Behind you it goes on shrieking at the world. Whether a cat finds it first or its mother does is not a thing your feet decided. You know that is true. You walk a little faster anyway.

events.text: You lie down for the night in a hollow of dry leaves under an oak, the softest bed on the hill, and the leaves squeak. Under them, a nest of field mice: a mother and six pink ones, blind, the size of your hoof's nail, and you are halfway down on top of them.

choices.text: Stop, and get up again very slowly

ok.log: You hold yourself up on trembling legs, halfway down, for as long as it takes to stand again without moving your weight. The mother mouse glares at you. All six are there. You sleep on the bare stones.

fail.log: Your legs give before you are up, and you come down a hand to the side, and there are five. You lie on the stones all night. You count them again in the morning, in case. There are five. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Lie down anyway: it is the softest bed on the hill (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You sleep well. In the morning the nest is empty and flattened and the mother is gone. You do not look closer. (Bent +1)

events.text: A traveller comes along the ledge path while you are lying at the edge of the ant road, waiting: a pedlar, with a pack. He stops. He looks at the red river, and at you, and then, without a word, he puts down his pack and kneels in the dust a pace away, and waits too. "My grandmother did this once," he says after a while, "at a gate. With something like you. The family always waits for ants. Nobody remembers why."

choices.text: Wait with him until the last ant

effects.log: You wait together until dusk, a scaled beast and a pedlar kneeling in the dust of a gorge. When the last ant has crossed, he gets up, knees cracking, and shoulders his pack. "There," he says. "Now I know why." He goes on down the path whistling.

choices.text: Touch his shoulder with your nose

effects.log: He goes very still. Then he laughs, softly, so as not to disturb the ants. "She said it was warm," he says. "She was right." Somewhere far back, in a life that was not yours, someone knelt beside something like you. It has come down a family like a habit of kindness.

events.text: {npc} tells you, sitting on the pasture fence, a story the old groom of the family tells: how once, as a small child in a threshing yard at dawn, the old groom put a bridle on a strange colt, and led it round once, and then took it off again because it was wrong. "It went up the hill without stepping on a stalk," says {npc}. "I would know it if I saw it, the story says." {He} looks at you, and at the halter in {his} hands, a long time.

choices.text: Put your head through the halter, and then take it out again

mem.note: did what the old story said

effects.log: In, and out, and you step back. {npc} laughs out loud, the way a child laughs when a story turns out to be true. "Like that," {he} says. "Exactly like that." {He} never tries the halter again.

choices.text: Walk away up the hill without stepping on a stalk

effects.log: {npc} watches you all the way up the slope. That evening {he} tells the old groom, who sits very still and then asks, twice, whether it stepped on anything. "Not one," says {npc}. The old groom nods for a long time.

events.text: A child from the village under the ridge, gathering windfall chestnuts in a basket, finds you under the same trees doing the same thing. The child stops. Then, very seriously, the child sets a heap of fallen chestnuts on a flat stone between you, unpeeled, and steps back. "Only the ones that fell," the child says. "My family says that is the rule, for your kind. Somebody in my family learned it, long ago."

choices.text: Eat from the heap

effects.log: You eat one. The child eats one. Neither of you takes one the other has peeled. It is the oldest table manners in the valley, and you did not know anyone else knew them. When you go, the child is still sitting by the stone, very satisfied.

choices.text: Push half the heap back to the child

effects.log: Half each. The child counts them, twice, and is satisfied that it is fair. Somebody, long ago, shared chestnuts with something like you, and a family has kept the rule ever since without knowing whom it was for.

events.text: While the village laughs at {npc}, an old woman from the end house comes to the kiln with a jar of barley water and says, loud enough for the oak wood to hear: "My grandmother saw one. A child ran and woke the whole village, and everyone laughed, and grandmother looked at the weed in the crack of the yard stone, standing straight, with hoofprints all round it. Grandmother never laughed. Don't you stop knowing."

choices.text: Step out of the oaks behind the old woman

mem.note: came out while the old woman spoke

effects.log: {npc} sees you over the old woman's shoulder and does not say a word. The old woman sees the look on that young face and does not turn round. "There," comes the dry old voice, and a hand pats {npc}'s hand, and the old woman goes home. Two of them know now. That is a great many, in a village.

choices.text: Stay in the oaks and let the old woman do it

effects.log: The old woman does it better than you could. Somebody once ran shouting through a village at dawn and was laughed at for it, and the laughter did not win. It has taken a long time to come back round to this kiln. It came back in time.
